name: Gareth Gupta

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government, and we don't sell or campaign. This conversation is confidential, including anything different from a public answer. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Gareth, 43, and I lead electrical work in homes and businesses. I've got a two-year technical diploma and a master electrician's licence, and I'm among the best practical workers in our firm. Today I found a fault in a shop's timer circuit, then showed the crew how to check the repair instead of trusting the label on the box. I like solving something properly and dislike searching through three old drawings to find the one that actually matches the installation.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What should I know about home and your use of new tools?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My partner checks other people's writing for mistakes as a freelance proofreader, and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I earn typical trade pay, we have about six weeks of expenses saved and some other electrical firms nearby, but my partner's customers have been slow paying recently. I use AI occasionally for job notes after a colleague has shown a tool works, checking the actual electrical details myself. I think paid learning and decent notice should be agreed together, instead of making each family buy its own way through a change.

I'd retain **proper repair time** and clear explanations alongside occasional checked note drafts.
think: The **proofreading receipts** don't always arrive when household bills do, keeping me worried despite my regular wage.
Our **six-week reserve** gives some room without stopping the mortgage and children's costs from arriving.
do: Cancel my **cinema pass** now and put its cost towards household bills.
Continue the **repair rota** through the first year and budget monthly from actual receipts rather than unpaid invoices.
feel: **Anxious** about household cash timing, with relief that the work itself remains familiar.

fieldNote: His **baseline anxiety** follows delayed second-income receipts and a moderate but short reserve, rather than automatically treating a plateau as household security.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew useful little tools could stay without the grand announcements. I'd keep an occasional checked note draft and still finish the actual repair properly. I'd want the same ordinary respect for the time it takes to explain a fault.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd still worry about the household account because the proofreading money doesn't always arrive when the bills do. Six weeks of expenses gives us something, but the mortgage and the children's needs keep arriving. A quiet AI story wouldn't make an overdue invoice arrive on time.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd cancel my adult cinema pass and put the cost towards household bills. In the first plateau year I'd keep the ordinary repair rota and occasional checked note drafts. I'd sit down with my partner monthly to use actual receipts, not unpaid invoices, in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about timing the money, with relief that both kinds of work carry on much as before. I'd still check the account before the mortgage payment. I wouldn't be frightened of a note tool that saved a few minutes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would cancelling the cinema pass change?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cancel mine before changing the children's regular activities. It would lower a bill, not replace a late client payment. I'd use the money for essentials rather than announce we'd suddenly increased savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if a client payment was still missing near mortgage day?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: We'd look at the actual gap together and ask the lender about options before missing a payment if necessary. I wouldn't promise a pause or a support payment we hadn't been approved for. I'd rather know the real limits than comfort the family with a guess.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we should check the new tools against actual jobs and agree what happens to paid time. I'd sign a crew request for paid preparation and proper instruction when a new system was required. I wouldn't want every saved minute to become somebody's unpaid evening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My practical repair wage could hold while my partner lost proofreading fees to cheap checking and rewriting. We'd feel that at home before a robot ever reached my van. I'd be uneasy using a handy note tool at work while the household's other work became harder to sell.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd sign the shared request for protected paid preparation and required teaching with colleagues. During the first year I'd learn the firm's approved AI drawing finder only after a colleague showed three correct archive matches, during paid work with normal hours and wages retained. I'd keep the cinema pass cancelled and compare actual household receipts monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household wage, though I wouldn't be afraid to try a tool that had been checked. I'd want to be useful without pretending the benefits were shared automatically. The mortgage sees the total money, not which adult earned it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check before using a drawing the tool found?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare the drawing with the actual installation and the approved record before relying on it. A correct filename isn't proof that the building still matches the drawing. If it picked a wrong version, I'd stop that use and show the colleague the example.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the crew request ask the owner to agree?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for paid preparation and instruction inside normal working hours, with basic wages protected, in writing. Signing the request wouldn't mean the owner had agreed. I wouldn't put a proposed protection into the household figures.

fieldNote: His **alarm** follows expected large household thinking-work losses in 2028, before the later robot stage reaches his own physical repairs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew thinking work changes in 2028 and capable hands-on robots follow around 2031. The proofreading income at home wouldn't get the physical trade's extra years. I'd still want paid-hour discussions before the changes, not only sympathy afterwards.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd expect most of my partner's proofreading fees to go when thinking work became that cheap and capable. My wage wouldn't cover all our ordinary commitments alone, and later robots could squeeze that wage too. I'd be awake trying to fit two household incomes into the space left by one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd keep the cinema pass cancelled and book free household advice with actual receipts, my wage and the mortgage figures. I'd sign the shared request for written paid-hour plans and paid required teaching, treating it as a proposal. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep the paid repair work and ask what lender or support options we actually qualified for, counting no relief or payment before approval.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed about a large household income loss in 2028, even while my own hands were still useful. I could still make the appointment and keep working. I'd need more than a task list to sleep easily.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you bring to the advice appointment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd put the actual receipts beside the bills with my partner before asking anyone for help. I'd want the adviser to explain what was eligible and what wasn't, including any lender limits. I wouldn't tell the children that submitting a form meant the house was already sorted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a career course straight away?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I wouldn't enrol either of us in a course we hadn't chosen, funded or checked against real work. I'd ask for paid practical instruction if my employer actually required a new system. The first task would be keeping the household budget honest.

In the first year after 2031 I'd keep the paid repair work, review receipts monthly and check lender and support options if income fell, assuming no approval or payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about money, with less pressure to guess both adults' next careers tonight. I'd have more time to ask a real question before spending. I wouldn't act as if the partner's fees were protected just because the date was later.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you avoid doing with the extra preparation time?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the adviser to use the actual receipts and explain where eligibility or lender terms put a limit on a plan. I'd rather keep the reserve available than spend it on a course chosen in a hurry. We haven't chosen one simply by talking about the risk.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If either wage weakened, we'd bring the budget discussion forward rather than wait for 2031. I'd keep the proposal separate from any written terms the employer actually agreed. The household needs the difference between a request and a wage to stay clear.

transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade gives us room to make several checked decisions instead of asking the family to pick one safe occupation forever. I'd still seek paid teaching when work actually required it. Thinking work in 2036 and robots around 2039 wouldn't make today's household bills wait.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 at the thinking change and around 56 when robots followed, still needing income unless our actual finances said otherwise. But my partner's fees could change much sooner, and six weeks of expenses would still be our present reserve. I can't live on either a future pension or an invoice the client hasn't paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer

transcript.speaker: persona

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money now, but less cornered about learning or changing something later. I'd want to enjoy time with the children without turning their interests into an emergency career plan. I'd still need the next year's receipts to improve in real life.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you change plans for the children now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I wouldn't decide their studies from this card or plan to live on their later wages. I'd tell them adults still ask for teaching and read the actual costs before accepting an opportunity. Their future shouldn't have to repair my household budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you check each year during the decade?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd compare actual paid hours, received fees and essential bills, then ask whether any promised work terms were really written and agreed. If income weakened earlier, we'd bring advice forward. A long warning doesn't make a delayed payment spendable.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because I expect most proofreading fees to go before my own practical work reaches the robot stage. Paid required teaching and honest written hours would help, alongside advice that used what clients actually paid. My master electrician's licence doesn't make my partner's unpaid invoice part of this month's mortgage money.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask which of the two adults gets hit first. My tools can still be in the van while the household has already lost a large part of its income. I'd want a plan that sees both jobs and the money actually arriving.
